extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners/searching authorities (ASEAN member states); patent office staff and practitioners performing searches and novelty assessments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting patent searches and assessing novelty (and related issues such as search reporting, scope, and enablement) for patent applications under ASEAN/PCT examination practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of documents cited in the application
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents cited in the application should be examined if they are cited as the starting point of the invention, or as showing the state of the art, as alternative solutions to the problem concerned, or when they are necessary for a correct understanding of the application; however, when such citations clearly relate only to details not directly relevant to the claimed invention, they may be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a cited document is unpublished or not accessible but appears essential, the searching authority may request the applicant to provide a copy if possible within time limits. If no copy is received, the searching authority should attempt the search and, where necessary, indicate that a meaningful search was not possible or had to be restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract and title consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner considers the abstract (together with the title of the invention and the figure of the drawings to be published with the abstract). Since the abstract should relate to the application as filed, the examiner should consider it and determine its definitive contents no later than the completion of the search report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abstract/title/figure to assist in defining and clarifying the subject matter for search purposes; finalize abstract contents by the time the search report is completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification according to IPC
rubrics_metrics.description: After having considered the abstract, if any, the examiner then classifies the application according to at least the International Patent Classification (IPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification should follow consideration of the abstract and support selection of appropriate search strategies and databases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search statement defining subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner may prepare a written search statement, defining the subject of their search as precisely as possible; claims may serve but may need to be generalized to cover all aspects and embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing the search statement, bear in mind exclusion-from-search issues and lack of unity. If unity is lacking, examiner may search only the first invention or inventive concept. Avoid restricting searches unless unavoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction and handling of lack of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner determines that unity of invention is not satisfied, the examiner may choose to conduct a search on the basis of the first invention or inventive concept only. The examiner may also have to restrict the search in exceptional situations because no search at all is possible, but they should not do this if it can be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting or performing partial/no search should be an exception. If description/claims/drawings are unclear to the extent that no meaningful search can be made, indicate 'no meaningful search' limited to exceptional situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of claim types and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims should be construed and searched having particular regard to the various types and forms of claims used, such as two-part claims and product-by-process claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt claim construction and search strategy to specific claim formats (e.g., product-by-process special guidance referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest prior art is that which in one single reference discloses the combination of features which constitutes the most promising starting point for a development leading to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a reference directed to similar purpose/effect or in same/closely related technical field; it should be capable of carrying out the function of the claimed invention and is chosen based on the examiner’s interpretation of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search focus: novelty, inventive step, sufficiency/support, industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner carries out the search, directing attention to any prior art likely to have bearing on novelty or inventive step. The examiner is encouraged to cite any prior art likely to be of assistance in determining sufficiency of description throughout the whole of the field claimed and the requirement that the claimed invention be fully supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify documents highly relevant to novelty, inventive step, adequacy of support, and industrial applicability; note documents important for priority validity or background but do not spend time searching for them unless special reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of post-dating documents for factual background
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents which do not qualify as prior art because they post-date the claimed invention may nevertheless be cited to show a universal fact, such as characteristics or properties of a material, or a specific scientific fact, or to show the level of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-dating documents can be used to establish general facts or skill level but not as novelty-destroying prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate search effort on high-probability resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should concentrate the search efforts on the search resources and strategies in which the probability of finding highly relevant documents is greatest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always consider search results already obtained when deciding to extend a search (e.g., additional databases, broaden queries, include classification places). Typically start with patent literature; in some areas search non-patent literature (NPL) if necessary; if little patent prior art is found, consider NPL databases.

rubrics_metrics.name: No special search for instantly well-known features
rubrics_metrics.description: No special search should be made for features that are instantly and unquestionably demonstrable as being well known such that documentary evidence is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferably cite a handbook or other document showing a feature is generally known if practicable, but do not expend special search effort for indisputably well-known features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner determination of novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner determines whether the claimed invention meets the standards for novelty and inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identified prior art, enablement analysis, PSIA framework and other criteria in subsequent novelty and inventive step assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents required in the search report
rubrics_metrics.description: The contents of the search report provided by the patent office should include at least: list and details of prior arts identified during the search, date of first publication/availability to the public, weblink when available; scope of the patent search; databases used; classification (IPC); summary of the search; relevance of prior art(s) to the claim(s); comments or written opinion from the examiner on patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure search report documents prior-art specifics, scope, methods and examiner's assessment/opinion to support subsequent examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial search and 'no search' options and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Options for a partial search and/or a 'no search' are available in AMS. The aim is to issue search reports as complete as possible but certain situations lead to no report or only a partial report (e.g., authority not required to handle subject-matter, or description/claims/drawings fail to meet requirements such that no meaningful search can be made).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'meaningful search' to mean complete enough to determine compliance with substantive requirements (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, sufficiency, support, clarity). Limit 'no meaningful search' to exceptional cases (totally unclear). If parts can be understood, perform search and recognize non-compliance may affect search extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of novelty (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim in a patent application is said to be novel if it is not anticipated by prior art. PCT: 'The invention, as defined by a claim, lacks novelty if every element or step is explicitly or inherently disclosed within the prior art including any features implicit to a person skilled in the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the standard that every element/step must be present in the prior art (explicitly or inherently) to destroy novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art (what counts as prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art includes everything made available to the public – anywhere in the world – through written disclosure (including drawings), use, oral disclosure, or any other way before the relevant date (national filing, international filing, or priority date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include internet disclosures and prior use/oral disclosures; the manner or geographical location of disclosure does not limit prior art under 'absolute novelty' regimes. Consider national variations and grace periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for determining scope via the Person Skilled In the Art (PSIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether an invention is new, the examiner shall compare the claimed invention to the identified prior art through the lens of a hypothetical 'Person Skilled In the Art' (PSIA) by (i) evaluating elements of the claim, (ii) determining if the prior art is part of the state of the art, and (iii) assessing whether each and every element or step was explicitly or inherently disclosed in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also consider the purpose/intended use of the invention in claim interpretation; disregard non-distinctive characteristics of intended use; consider implied characteristics arising from particular use (examples: catalyst vs dye; 'mould for molten steel' implies limitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute novelty and grace periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally universal or absolute novelty is required; claims must be novel compared to any prior art published or used anywhere. All AMS except Thailand apply 'absolute novelty'. AMS provide a grace period preventing some disclosures from becoming prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No age restriction on prior art; admissions by applicant can constitute prior art but presumption can be rebutted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet disclosures as prior art and date reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet/on-line database disclosures are considered like other written disclosure and are publicly available as of the date the disclosure was publicly posted. Password protection or payment does not prevent a web page from forming part of the state of the art if it was in principle available without confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish publication date and accessibility; in many cases accept internet publication dates at face value unless applicant provides reasons to the contrary. Consider degrees of reliability; burden of proof on applicant to show date incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit/inherent disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art disclosure may be implicit/inherent; implicit/inherent teachings can be considered part of the prior art and hence destroy novelty, but should be raised only where there can be no reasonable doubt as to the practical effect of the prior teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inherent disclosure approach rather than a purely 'photographic' explicit-only approach. Only find lack of novelty on implicit teaching when PSIA would inevitably arrive at the claimed subject-matter in carrying out the prior teaching (example: rubber's elastic properties implying 'elastic material').

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical equivalents treated under inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty involves whether the prior art discloses each and every feature specified in the claim. If the claim contains technically equivalent or additional features, many AMS recommend that an objection of obviousness (inventive step) would be more appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate technical equivalents with novelty in jurisdictions that treat equivalents under inventive step; follow national legislation/guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-prejudicial disclosures / exceptions to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures are not part of the state of the art if they occurred within a specific grace period for disclosures by the inventor/applicant (or predecessor) or occurred due to abuse of rights or if information was contained in an application disclosed mistakenly by the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply statutory grace period provisions and exceptions cited in formalities guidance when determining prior art status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation of alternatives/Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim contains alternatives, for example Markush claims (P1, P2, P3 ... Pn), any alternatives disclosed in the prior art are anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check each alternative in prior art; the disclosure of any claimed alternative anticipates that alternative of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant date(s) for assessing prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'relevant date' for considering prior art is the national filing date or the international filing date or, where priority is validly claimed, the date of priority. Different claims or different alternatives in one claim may have different relevant dates depending on priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty against each claim (or each part/alternative) using its own relevant date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and assumptions about the PSIA
rubrics_metrics.description: The PSIA is a hypothetical person having ordinary skill in the art and being aware of what was common general knowledge at the relevant date. The PSIA is presumed to have access to prior art (including documents cited in the search report) and the normal means and capacity for routine experimentation. In some advanced technologies, it may be appropriate to think in terms of a group rather than a single person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor PSIA assumptions to the technology; assume routine experimentation and access to common knowledge and cited documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement for prior art to destroy novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art disclosure must enable a PSIA to carry out the claimed invention. A prior art document that is not enabling for the claimed invention does not destroy novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the prior art, together with knowledge generally available on the effective date, enables preparation/separation or practice of the claimed subject-matter. When considering NPL raising enablement questions, take appropriate outside knowledge into account. Note: non-enabling prior art may still be relied upon for inventive step analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of single document vs combining documents for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, a single prior art document is to be considered in determining whether novelty is lacking. However, in specific cases (e.g., primary document explicitly refers to a second document available at the relevant time) the teachings of the second may be regarded as incorporated; additional documents may be used as evidence of sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not combine separate items from different embodiments in the same document unless the combination has been specifically suggested. Rely on incorporation-by-reference only where the primary document refers to the secondary and that secondary was publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic vs specific disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic disclosure does not usually take away the novelty of any specific example falling within that disclosure; conversely, a specific disclosure takes away the novelty of any generic claim embracing that disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the prior art's generic teaching specifically or implicitly discloses the claimed specific example; many AMS adopt this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of ranges for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Guiding principles when examining whether ranges are anticipated: (1) a specific example in the prior art within a claimed range anticipates the range; (2) prior art teaching a range overlapping/touching the claimed range may anticipate if it discloses the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity'; (3) a prior art broader range may not anticipate a narrow claimed range if the narrow range is a selection invention supported by evidence (e.g., unexpected results); (4) prior art ranges or values very close to but not overlapping the claimed range do not anticipate the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of 'sufficient specificity' is case-specific. Consider examples and jurisdictional nuances (e.g., Singapore, Viet Nam, Indonesia guidance). For selection inventions, unexpected results and narrowness/specificity support novelty; very close but non-overlapping values leave novelty intact but require inventive step analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second medical use claims and pharmaceutical exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims over a new medical use of a known medicine ('second use claims') arise in countries allowing pharmaceutical product patents. Claims in the form 'Use of substance or composition X for the treatment of disease Y...' may be regarded as relating to a method for treatment (which is explicitly excluded from patentability by some AMS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of national differences: some AMS exclude product patents for pharmaceuticals; treatment-method claims may be excluded. Apply national guidance on allowable claim formats for second medical use (and alternatives where product patents are allowed).
